fields.title: Standup Is Not for Reporting
fields.keyTakeaway: A standup answers one question: where reality diverged from the plan. Everything not about divergence is an activity report, and you can skip it.
fields.checkQuestion: Everyone took turns sharing what they did yesterday. What did you learn from this about sprint risks?
fields.blocks/0/text: Key node question: **how much does the actual state differ from the plan?** Not "who is doing what," but specifically the divergence — because action is required only on that.
fields.blocks/1/text: **What happens if you don't answer the question.** The problem is discovered on the last day of the sprint. It existed for four days, but no one said it out loud: everyone individually hoped to make it in time.
fields.blocks/2/subtitle: Fifteen minutes, three questions, one purpose
fields.blocks/2/items/0: **What moved since yesterday** — not "what I did," but what changed on the board.
fields.blocks/2/items/2: **What is at risk** — which sprint task already looks unrealistic.
fields.blocks/2/items/3: Rule: discussions about divergence are moved **after** the standup and only with those involved.
fields.blocks/3/text: The difference between "what I did" and "what moved" seems verbal, but it changes everything. Everyone always has the first one. The second can be empty — and that emptiness is precisely the signal.
fields.blocks/4/text:
The "what I did" format: "worked on synchronization," "worked on synchronization," "worked on synchronization." Three days in a row, everything sounds fine.

The "what moved" format: "nothing, third day struggling with the scanner returning codes with a delay on old Androids."

The second phrasing is a signal a week before the end of the sprint. The first is a day before.
fields.blocks/5/text: A standup reveals divergence but does not fix it: if nothing happens after it, it turns into a ritual. And it is useless where people are afraid to admit they are stuck — in that case, it is not the meeting that needs fixing.
